speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minisier of Naiional Defence):
maintopic: ARCTIC ISLANDS-REPORTED SELECTION OF LANDING STRIPS BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last the hon. member for Laurier referred to a recent news report to the effect that the United States had picked out some 50 emergency landing strips in the Canadian Arctic islands for military and civilian planes. He asked if the statement was factual and whether there were any conditions governing the use of these fields, and I told him I would get a report. The answer is as follows.
The report apparently referred to a United States study entitled "Terrain Analysis of Ice Free Land sites in Arctic Canada" dated February, 1961. As part of the United States arctic research program a study was performed during 1960-61 with the assistance of Canadian Aero Service Limited of Ottawa. The major purpose of this project was the identification, location and preliminary terrain analysis of the most promising ice free natural landing sites within the Canadian Arctic, north of the 65th parallel. The study was based entirely on an examination of aerial

photographs taken by the R.C.A.F. and readily available to the general public through the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. It indicated that there are some 50 sites within the area where landing strips could readily be developed.
The results of the study have been made available to the Canadian government departments concerned, and through the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to interested commercial companies. To date there are no plans for the development or utilization of these possible landing strips.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

If an answer were given outside of the house to a question which was not answered in the house, that might raise the question of the rights of the house or of hon. members. subtopic: MR. MCILRAITH  DELAY IN ANSWERING QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER

(Text):
The house resumed, from Thursday, February 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for the second reading of Bill No. C-49, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act.

Mr. Speaker, when the house was debating this resolution some time ago I traced the history of this legislation and tried to indicate that this was one of the four great measures brought forward by this government a year ago last fall as the four corners of the great edifice against unemployment, along with the Vocational Training Act, the amendments to the National Housing Act, and there was one
Small Businesses Loans Act other piece of legislation that went along with those whereby unemployment was to be combated.
This government came into power, at least in part, on its promise to help the small businessman, and it set up a small business department in the Department of Trade and Commerce. The only thing about this department is that it remained small, and I cannot really see that it has helped the small businessman very much. The first year it appeared in the estimates with a grant of some $30,000. Last year it received nothing. I looked in vain this year in the estimates-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member must realize that is quite wrong. The appropriation for the small business loans branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce is there in the estimates. It is included in a larger item now. This was discussed on the estimates in the last session.

What the minister is really saying is that it has been absorbed and has now appeared as a part of another section, but I think we can say that this department has made no real, significant change in the way this government has dealt with the small businessman since the last election.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a silly statement; it is not true.
It is true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is untrue.

Supposedly this measure for loans to the small businessman was to provide a great pool of some $300 million government guaranteed, and strangely enough the small businessmen across this nation refused to dip into this pool except to the extent of some $27 million.
I am sure hon. members on the other side of the house realize that the availability of capital is the most important aspect of taking part in business today.
A few days ago I was reading a little book by two men called Adler and Kelso. They were the authors of a book which caused quite a furore sometime ago entitled "The Capitalist Manifesto". This new little book is called "The New Capitalists". I think it should be read by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house who are going to fight the next election on the basis of free enterprise and maintaining our capitalist system. These authors say that our system is going down, and the main problem is that the large capitalist can finance his day to day activities by acquiring more capital, in comparison with the man who has to go into the open market to get it. The advantage is always with the large corporation to the

Small Businesses Loans Act disadvantage of the small business. To put it bluntly, those who have will get more, and those who have not will get less.
Of course as time goes by capital is going to be more important than labour. The importance of labour as compared with capital is declining year by year. These authors look ahead for many years and see a situation whereby the capital of the nation will be controlled and concentrated in fewer and fewer hands. They say this is wrong, and that if we are to stop this happening we must take a very great leap forward. The solution of the author is to make everyone a capitalist, and he calls it the new capitalism. He points out that we must use the insurance principle to deal with the problem of entrepreneurial error which makes it almost impossible for the small investor to take a chance.
This bill is in a sense trying to do somewhat the same thing; it is within this area. It is taking a direct approach and placing capital in the hands of those who need it. The small businessman, as we have seen, is driven constantly to the loan company, to high interest rates, to restrictive terms. The important thing about this piece of legislation is that although it looks good on paper, it simply is not fulfilling its purpose.
A recent article in the Globe and Mail of Tuesday, February 6 indicated that there are some 64,000 small businesses and small manufacturing firms which have assets of less than $250,000 and which come within the purview of this legislation. This is multiplied, of course, when we take into account those businesses which are in the service, retail and the tourist fields, all the areas which this broad piece of legislation was expected to cover, of which only some 2,000 have taken advantage of this legislation.
Some 3,000.
Well, between 2,000 and 3,000.
Twenty seven million dollars out of $300 million.

I know one bank in Peterborough which is absolutely surrounded by small businesses; it is one of the oldest banks in the city, but it does not have one single loan on its books under this legislation. I know another bank where they have had some 25 requests, not one of which came within the demands of this legislation. I tried to get information on this bill. I think if hon. members will look at Hansard, page 1243, and the questions I put on small business loans they will see how I tried to get information which I felt was extremely important if we were to judge this piece of legislation and

look at the measure with which we are now dealing with some kind of knowledge. I asked question No. 175;
What was the total amount of money lent under last session's Bill No. C-40 (Small Businesses Loans Act) in the year 1961?
The answer was $25,582,269.41. My second question was:
How many loans were made during 1961 under
the said act?
How many loans were made in amounts from (a) up to $500 (b) $500 to $1,000 (c) $1,000 to $5,000-
And so on. In other words I wanted a breakdown of the number of loans and the amounts loaned under this legislation. That information was unavailable. Perhaps the Minister of Finance could tell us why this kind of information is not available on what I consider to be an extremely important piece of legislation. There is no breakdown of the loans which have been made under this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can answer the hon. member right now.
We are not in committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This information has not been broken down in this form as yet. I am told it would take at least two weeks to break down the information we have into the detailed categories the hon. member set forth in his question.

I wish the minister had mentioned that at the time, because simply saying that the information is not available would lead one to believe that it was not going to be made available. My next question was:
How many applications were (a) received (b) rejected?
Once again this information is not available.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government has not got that information; that is information the banks have. They receive the applications; they deal with them and accept or reject them. The government is given information only as to loans that are allowed to which the government guarantee applies.

I thank the minister for that information, but it would seem to me that if the government is going to have any complete view as to how effective this legislation really is to the small businessman, this is the kind of information it would be very well to get from the bankers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You cannot.

It seems to me that if we are to be able to tell whether the small businessman can really benefit by this kind of legislation, these government guaranteed loans,

surely we should know how many are being rejected because they do not come within the purview of this legislation. It would seem to me, on the basis of the comments I have heard from many people, that this is simply not getting through. Last year when we talked about the industrial development bank I was heartened by the fact that at least two members spoke up and said there should be a more liberal policy, that there should be more inclination to take a chance when making advances to industries applying to this government agency for loans. That surely is the view I might have expected would have been taken with regard to this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is quite different.

I fail to see how it is quite different, and I say so in the sense that here again the government is trying to make credit available to smaller groups, though in relation to the industrial development bank they were trying to make capital available to the larger companies.
I would refer the minister to the remarks he made when he introduced this legislation in the house as reported in Hansard at page 55, 1960. It was suggested then that the expectation was that the government guarantee would encourage lending and increase the availability of medium term credit to small business. The minister then seemed to be very interested in comparing this legislation with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. He said- and I am quoting from page 55 of Hansard:
The general nature of the legislation is similar to the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
He went on to say it was similar in form to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Then he added:
It has been represented to us by small business organizations that the amount of contract work available in the course of renovation and extension of premises of small retail businesses in Canada amounts to approximately $75 million.
Yet, we find that the total loans made under this act for that year amounted to only $25 million. Let us look at the results of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. In 1960 some 68,041 loans were made under the terms of that act. Under this legislation 2,977 loans were made. In that period $101 million was lent under the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Under this act the amount made available was $25 million. Let us look at the size of the loans. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act the average size of the loans made was $1,497. Under the Small Businesses Loans Act it was $8,593. I think it was the hon. member for Ottawa West who dealt with the whole question of putting the number of companies at the top.
Small Businesses Loans Act What is happening to the people at the bottom? It seems to me that $8,593 is rather a high average for loans to small businesses. I wonder what has happened to the grocery store owner, the motel owner, the small businessman who will only need one or two thousand dollars. I am sorry we do not have a breakdown of these loans so we could see what has happened to the people at the bottom.
I do not think I need go over the statements which have been made by the hon. member for Welland in this respect. Those we are trying to cover in this legislation are those who have managed to survive the last three years of Conservative recession, and those who hope to survive the next few years. This measure obviously does not cover those people. One person who is closely associated with banking has said of this that it looks good but it does not seem to cover the people he serves. This man is surrounded by small businesses. Small businesses have been very badly hit by this recession. They have suffered far more than the large corporations. They cannot create their own capital, and they are dependant entirely on the market place for their credit. Now they find that these regulations are too stringent.
Here again the problem is not just one for the bankers. What the banker does is determined by a conservative finance policy, conservative with a small "c". He has to make sure that his money will come back, and he has to be more than sure under the terms of this legislation. Yet surely this government must recognize its responsibility for having created an economy which has been to the detriment of the small businessman. The fact is that the small businessman, like the small farmer, has found his position destroyed by the recession, and is no longer able to compete on a practical basis.
I am trying to be constructive this afternoon. Perhaps we could look to the Department of Agriculture for some guidance concerning how to make this bill of real assistance to the small businessman who really needs help. I look with some interest at the work of the Farm Credit Corporation. We have a small businessman's section already in operation in one of our departments; the minister and I disagree as to how effective it has been. But it is in this area that I wish to suggest a direction in which improvements might be made. A tremendous effort could be made in terms of enlarging the scope of this section, even to the point where its officials could go into an area, talk with those concerned, find out what money is needed, find how a business is operating and what help is really required as a basis for
1470	HOUSE OF
Small Businesses Loans Act giving the businessman concerned some assistance in improving his enterprise and making it really worth while, as is done by officials of the Farm Credit Corporation. That organization does not simply say "It looks as if we shall not get our money back here, so we will let this applicant go without it and get along as well as he can". The small businessman needs help and advice as well as credit.
Some may say that this sounds like socialism. I do not think so. I think it is a sensible way of dealing with this problem. I think small business is in a bad way, and we must take its problems into account. I hope this government will take a different look at the difficulties now confronting the small businessmen of our nation.

As an
advocate of long standing for greater consideration by lending institutions to small businesses, I welcome the amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act before us which extends the availability of loans to include the construction or purchase of other premises, if the premises in which the business now conducted cease to be available, or if it is considered advisable to move to other locations or extend facilities to enable the expansion of business. I doubt whether there is a class of business, outside of small farmers, who are more deserving of consideration than these businessmen whose contribution accounts for 60 per cent of the internal trade of Canada, to say nothing of their individual contribution to the welfare and public life of the community in which they live. Often they give much of their personal service gratis, at no small sacrifice.
I would like to point out the contribution made by the tourist camp and motel operators to the wealth of our nation. The tourist industry has reached a status of great importance to the economy of Canada. Only wheat and newsprint bring in more money from outside Canada than do tourists. Only newsprint brings in more money from the United States than does the tourist industry. It benefits Canada in many ways.
I think it is sound to recognize the tourist business for what it really is. Figures show that it is one of the major Canadian industries. In spite of considerable expansion in motel and tourist resort promotion we are still far behind the United States in tourist facilities, not because of a lack of qualified persons eager to go into the business but because those people who are really interested cannot get the money to start a business.
The recently completed lake Superior circle super highway, which follows the lake from Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, south to Michigan,


Wisconsin and Minnesota, and finally Fort William, is 1,200 miles of scenic splendour, but unfortunately the Canadian side lacks the accommodation for the thousands of tourists who are coming in an ever increasing all year round calvacade to enjoy such inspiring sights as only the rugged shores of lake Superior can provide. It creates additional business and employment. Our tourist operators can hold Canadians in Canada and keep in circulation here money which would otherwise be spent abroad.
Travel by Canadians within Canada promotes a deeper understanding and appreciation of their own country and fosters national unity. In other words, tourism benefits everybody.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I wonder whether the hon. member would consider that he has sufficiently expounded all the virtues of the tourist industry to bring them within the purview of this act. We are really not debating the tourist industry. It is true that we are debating small business in the tourist field in so far as this amendment is concerned, but I suggest it does not open the door to a general review of the tourist industry.

Mr. Speaker, on the point of order, with due deference to Your Honour's opinion on the matter, we are speaking about small business and I consider the small operators in the tourist industry to be engaged in small business. That is the way I view the matter. I submit it is the course of wisdom on our part to keep our tourist operators in business in order to retain the tourist dollar in the country.
I submit that in referring to the tourist business in discussing this amendment I am merely emphasizing the need of the small operator who is a small businessman. With respect, I submit I am quite in order in speaking on behalf of the tourist operator who, after all, is a small businessman. Those who provide the tourist accommodation required to meet the increased demand are entitled to the assistance which this amendment is supposed to provide. Today the tourist industry is developing from what it used to be-camp resorts offering cabin type of accommodation-to up to date modern establishments, because tourists demand accommodation equal to that which is provided by modern hotels.
Most visitors come to Canada from the United States by automobile, and this mode of travel creates a greater demand for roadside accommodation of the highest quality. Although many motels have been built in recent years, a substantial percentage of

Canada's motels and cabins needs to be improved and enlarged. There have also been sharp increases in tourism by Canadians visiting vacation spots in Canada. While no complete information is available concerning interprovincial travel, it seems fairly clear that the value of travel by Canadians within Canada is of an importance equal to that of the tourist business from the United States.
The expansion and improvement of Canada's tourist establishments, which include resorts, restaurants, hotels, motels and camps, are urgently required. At present the facilities which are inadequate and outmoded are being compared unfavourably with the more modern establishments which the travelling tourist expects, and the modernization of many of these businesses requires capital which quite often the operator is unable to borrow through ordinary banking facilities. This applies, of course, to tourist resorts and motels which, by reason of the relocation of highways, have to be removed to other locations.
I realize that with the passing of the government sponsored bill last year, No. C-40, provision was made for government guaranteed loans by chartered banks to small businesses, which has been of some help to small business enterprises for improvement and modernization of equipment and premises. However, some small businesses have encountered difficulties, notwithstanding the act, resulting in refusals by the banks to grant reasonable term credit to these proprietors of small businesses.
The minister has pointed out in reply to the hon. member for Peterborough that the department has no record of applications to the chartered banks under this legislation. This is an important omission. Surely the government should be kept informed as to the number of loans approved and the amounts, and also the number of applications for loans which were rejected. I dare say that the latter is greater than the former.
The major problems of the small retailer are a shortage of adequate long term capital and a shortage of well trained personnel. The small business is a major factor in the Canadian economy. The late Henry Ford staunchly declared that the small businessman was the backbone of the nation, which is just as true today as it was in Henry Ford's time.
Small businesses can be likened to a barometer which measures the economic climate of the country. Let us consider the impact on the national economy if the approximately 450,000 small businesses, including retailers, tourist operators, small service operators employing from 2 to 15 to 20 persons, were able 26207-1-94
Small Businesses Loans Act to hire one or two more. There would be a business boom which would practically eliminate our present serious unemployment problem.
It is a pity that when the government established the productivity council the small independent business was ignored, notwithstanding the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that the legislation provided for representation of all sectors of the economy. As far as I know, big business and the labour congress are the only groups represented on that body.
Good as this amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act is, small business in Canada deserves greater recognition. The small tourist camp operators and motel owners and the independent stores are the real custodians of the principle of free enterprise. Here we see at first hand the workings of the profit and loss system. Here we see the reward of success, invariably made possible by recognition of efficiency, resourcefulness, hard work and integrity.
Notwithstanding the growth and expansion of big business, which is a trend developed by large investments, small business will continue to exist and be the mainstay of free enterprise because of the opportunity it offers for ingenuity, initiative and love for work. I cannot think of a better champion of democracy than the businessman who is self employed and knows the names of all his employees and many of his customers.
These are the people whom this bill is designed to assist. I submit that they deserve even more consideration than the bill contains. Some form of long term financing is needed to help those who wish to expand or relocate their premises. More than once I have had the opportunity to observe long established small independent businesses driven to the wall and into bankruptcy because of lack of sufficient capital to improve services and expand their holdings. They were unable to compete with large chain stores; their cheery personal services are gone and, sad to say, with them a part of the economic backbone of the nation is also gone.
In addition to lack of capital, small business establishments are handicapped by discriminatory freight rates in sections of the country such as northwestern Ontario, where horizontal freight rate increases over the past 10 years have driven to the verge of ruin many businesses, small and large.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have refrained from rising previously on a point of order in the hope that perhaps the hon. gentleman might get back in order, as you suggested. However, he is now talking about freight rates. He has talked about everything

Small Businesses Loans Act else except this bill. With great respect I suggest that there ought to be insistence that he conform to the rules and discuss the bill.

t
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Again I am obliged to say that freight rate discrimination has an adverse effect on small business establishments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Order.

I am merely pointing out the situation. I am going to say this. This amendment is designed to help and assist the small businessman. I am trying to point out a way in which to assist him. I know the difficulties the small businessmen are confronted with in the form of any discrimination. In any event I am in favour of the amendment. I do not wish to prolong the debate on it. I think we all agree, with some reservations. It should go a little further. We should know the number of people who have applied and were turned down. We should know the amount of money invested in these small businesses and guaranteed by the government. I think it would assist the government a great deal, and also assist the small businessman.
For my part I am in favour of the amendment, notwithstanding the fact that it does not go far enough. However, I am sure that those who have been unable to borrow money under the old act will now try again. I express the hope that they will receive fairer consideration and will be able to borrow sufficient to meet their needs under this present legislation.

This legislation has come before the house two or three times this session, Mr. Speaker. While I had not intended to speak on it, I believe that up to this time two things have been overlooked. I wholeheartedly support the amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act. As to a businessman who has an established business,


and who for one reason or another finds it necessary to move his location, this amendment will allow him to borrow in order to make the move.
The hon. member for Peterborough went to great lengths in comparing this particular measure with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. They are similar in many respects. He said that while under this measure, which has been in effect for one year, $25 million is lent, that was a small amount having regard to the principal with which it was set up, namely $300 million. He compared it to the $75 million lent under the Farm Improvement Loans Act in 1960. However, it must be remembered that this act has been in effect just a shade better than a year, and at the time of the figures he was using it had only been in effect one year. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, in the first year in which it was in effect, approximately 4,000 loans were made and $3,381,000 lent.
I think it is only fair to compare like years in respect of one act with like years in respect of the other, if you are going to draw a comparison. When the Farm Improvement Loans Act was set up the aggregate principal amount was $250 million. While they are similar acts, certainly the Small Businesses Loans Act has been readily accepted and has made a substantial contribution to small business and to the men in business. If this act continues to grow in the way the Farm Improvement Loans Act has grown since its inception back in 1944, it will continue to play a great part in the development of this country.
The hon. member for Peterborough went on to say that the average amount lent under the Small Businesses Loans Act was $8,500, and he compared this with the average amount lent under the Farm Improvement Loans Act which was $1,400. However, he did not know or did not realize that while a farmer may have several farm improvement loans at one time, his total amount in any one year may be up to $7,500 under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I suggest that most farmers would be paying on possibly an average of $4,500. I am just taking that figure out of my own general knowledge of my own area. Under the Small Businesses Loans Act I am sure it would be more than likely that a small businessman would have one loan, and that would be the average of $8,500. I think the averages compare rather well, considering also the fact that under the Small Businesses Loans Act the businessman can borrow up to a maximum of $25,000 if his business is large enough.
The hon. member tried to portray to the house and to you, Mr. Speaker, a picture showing that the Small Businesses Loans Act

was not going to play a part in the development of Canada and was not going to meet the condition which it was first thought it would meet. By comparisons he tried to portray this picture, by comparing the effect of this act with the effective part the Farm Improvement Loans Act has played over the years in helping out a great many farmers. I submit that he made a very poor comparison when he sought to compare the figures for the very first year of operation of this new piece of legislation with the last figures available for a well established piece of legislation which the farmers have become accustomed to using a great deal.
I think I have pointed out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that the Small Businesses Loans Act compares very favourably with other legislation, and I think it will go on to play a major part in the development and continuing expansion of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the remarks just made by the hon. member for Acadia. Among his contentions I noted his claim that this legislation had made a substantial contribution to the welfare of small business in Canada. I may not be using his exact words, but I believe I am quoting him with reasonable accuracy. I submit that this act has made a substantial contribution to the welfare of our banking system and the chartered banks of Canada, because under the terms of the act they have been making loans that in all likelihood they would have made in any case. They have been happy to enjoy the benefits of this legislation. Any rather marginal loans they made in the past are now in effect insured by the government of Canada; therefore they do not need to run any substantial risk with regard to the loans they make.
I say this with the particular thought in mind that according to the terms of the legislation the banks are still entitled to collect the maximum rate of interest permissible under the provisions of the Bank Act. We have heard many comparisons of this act with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. However, there is an important distinction. If the government of Canada underwrites a loan made under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the guarantee of the government of Canada has the effect of reducing the interest rate that the borrower must pay. This condition does not apply in the case of the Small Businesses Loans Act. While the government likes to compare this legislation with the Farm Improvement Loans Act, I regret very much that it has not seen fit to insist that the guarantee by the government 26207-1-94J
Small Businesses Loans Act should merit a reduction in the maximum allowable interest rate. I would hope that the government would heed the advice we gave it when it first introduced this legislation and bring in an amendment to establish a maximum interest rate for any loans made under the terms of this act, in line with the maximum rate now applicable to loans made under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. After all, the bond of the people of Canada should be worth something. Having in mind that the banks are permitted to collect 6 per cent interest on risks that they assume entirely, if they receive a guarantee by the people of Canada with regard to a major portion of any loan under this act I feel this should warrant a reduction of the maximum interest rate that the banks are able to collect.
By the government's failure to establish a maximum interest rate permitted to the banks of Canada under the terms of this legislation it is in effect announcing to all and sundry that the word of the government of Canada does not mean very much. The government is in fact saying to the banks "You can make loans on your own or you can make loans with our guarantee. Do as you please; you can collect the same rate of interest in either case". Naturally the banks are going to take the guarantee. In fairness and justice to the taxpayers of Canada and also in the interests of the small businessmen of Canada, I believe that if we guarantee loans by legislation the maximum permissible interest rate should be reduced.
I should like to endorse the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Fort William. I have encountered many operators of tourist camps or trailer camps who find themselves without adequate facilities under either the Industrial Development Bank Act or the Small Businesses Loans Act. Anyone who cares to read the Financial Post for January 27 will see that the editors of the Financial Post, who in these days seem to be about the only people left in the journalistic world who view this government with any charity at all, were led to expect some real legislation, some real changes that would lift this legislation from the doldrums in which it has found itself, with only $25 million lent when they expected $300 million and, as one hon. member has pointed out, probably most of it would have been lent anyway whether or not the legislation had been there. As my friend the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo has said, this legislation is so different from what we were led to expect, is so different from what the public was led to expect and is in so many ways inadequate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He did not say that.

We had expected that something really substantial would be done, something that would carry out some of those sweeping promises to small business that were made by the Prime Minister in his election campaign in 1957 and which I could put on the record-I have them here in my hand- if the rules of the house would allow it. However, I see you looking at me, Mr. Speaker. There seems to be distaste on the other side of the house for having any of these promises of the Prime Minister put on the record, even in the most attenuated form. Objection is taken even to having quotation marks put around them. As I say, what we were led to expect was that legislation would be put on the statute books which, like the farm improvement legislation and the other legislation such as the home improvement legislation, which was put on the statute books by another government in another period, would have much more substantial effects than this legislation is having. Surely what was expected was something like the measures that are being taken by the small businesses administration in the United States to which the Prime Minister referred when he made the promises on which this legislation evidently is based, or which this legislation is supposed or presumed to be fulfilling. When he replies I hope the minister will tell us whether the government has given any consideration to a much broader approach to this whole problem than the miserable approach that is made in this puny amendment to legislation which is not really accomplishing what everyone a year and a half ago had such high hopes it might accomplish.
In the United States, of course, many devices are being used for providing capital for small business. For example, there are small business investment companies.
There are 21 different projects.
My friend the hon. member for Essex East, who has made a real study of this matter, points out that there are 21 different projects.

You have not made a
study of it?

I do not pretend to be an authority on the whole field. However, I pretend to know something about what is going on in Canada. I also know something about the number of loans being made under this legislation in Canada. That information has been given very reluctantly by the government. I have this circular from the small business administration in October, 1961,

which suggests what I believe looks like a much more promising approach to this problem than is this legislation. It is for that reason, and for that reason only-that I consider this legislation so inadequate-that I venture to suggest to the minister that a more promising measure such as that to which I have referred might be considered. I mean promising in the sense of achieving results not in the electoral field but in the field of the growth of the economy. We know, of course, that many promises seem to be made and forgotten. But the kind of promise I am talking about is the promise of effective results in the development of small businesses. I think that only one conclusion can be drawn from the few facts that we have been able to elicit from the minister and the brutal fact of the small number of loans, namely that this measure is all right as far as it goes but that it does not go nearly far enough to meet the big problem which the Prime Minister, when he was not in the government, promised to do so much about in 1957.

The hon.
member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) referred to some of the promises that were made in 1957 with respect to this group of citizens, namely the small businessman. In Brockville, on May 8, 1957, according to the Globe and Mail of May 9, we have this quotation:
The small businessman-manufacturer and independent retailer-has been all but forgotten by the federal government, the Tory chief charged . ..
Canada, Mr. Dlefenbaker's statement said, is a country of small businesses. Of the 37,400 manufacturing establishments in this country, more than 35,000 employ fewer than 100 persons.
There was also specific reference on that occasion and on the earlier occasion of the important opening campaign speech at Massey hall to the type of legislation under the United States program, where the definition of small business is flexible enough to permit aid to be extended to any firm which is small when judged within its own industry. We submit there should be further amendments and more real legislation at this time.
In the second quarter of 1961 the number of business failures resulted in liabilities of $27.7 million, 11 per cent above the same months in the same quarter of 1960. This was an all-time high. Nineteen per cent more firms failed in January, 1962, than in January, 1961, and in this regard I am referring to a news story found on page 22 of today's Globe and Mail.

Why do you not give the
reasons for the failures?

In answer to the hon. member for Edmonton West I will give the reasons
Small Businesses Loans Act for the failures. The Financial Post says that the reasons are primarily three: First, a general slowdown in business. This we cannot deny. The second reason is the high cost of borrowing. This goes back to the reconversion loan and the manipulations that have been going on fairly generally since then as a result of which there has been a buildup of the average cost of interest on all debts from 2.98 per cent prevailing in 1956 to a figure we cannot accurately judge at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, this must be the dozenth time the debate has been out of order and surely we can have some serious attempt made to confine the debate within the proper rules. It has been straying all afternoon. The hon. member is now talking about interest rates in general, about the conversion loan of 1958 and everything else except the principle of the bill. The principle is very simple, whether the permissible purposes for which loans may be guaranteed under the act shall be extended to include removal and relocation of businesses.
Mr. Speaker, may I say word?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not necessary. I cannot accept the objection. It seems to me that hon. member is relating his argument to borrowing by small businesses, which has to do with the provision that is being amended. I would not want to restrict him as long as he does not get into the whole policy of reconversion and so on. It is obvious that would not be in order, but when his remarks are related to borrowings by small businesses it seems to me he is on the point.

Mr. Speaker, I was endeavouring to reply briefly and succinctly to the hon. member for Edmonton West. I mentioned that, according to the Financial Post, the second most important item was the high cost of borrowing. This added cost is surely one of the main reasons why there has been an increase in business failures. The third reason put forward by the Financial Post is the obvious scarcity of mortgage money.
May I say it would appear that within the last four or five years we have entered into a new period of debt morality, and this has to be taken into account when we are considering the legislation before the house today. So far as the debts of the government are concerned, it is clear there is no earnest attempt to balance the budget. In other words, obviously we have entered into a new phase so far as the problem of meeting the costs of government is concerned. Our biggest business, Canadian National Railways, has a

Small Businesses Loans Act record deficit, and we do not try to balance the budget in this particular field. We do not try to balance the unemployment insurance fund. The financial position of T.C.A. and our exchange fund are two other areas where we could draw comparisons.
These policies pursued by the government are beyond our understanding. All we can do is to testify that we have witnessed all these things. Why these things are so, I do not know, but certainly this new debt morality in Canada is one of the factors that profoundly affects small businesses which have to borrow, which either have to pay or get out of business. It is as simple as that, and the manner in which the government has pursued its fiscal and monetary policies has had an important bearing on the way small businesses can operate. If our big government undertakings, our railway system, our air line system and so on, are to be permitted to go substantially into debt, I think it is only reasonable to say that the ground root strength of our economy the merchant and small businessman, has got to be supplied with a little more food and water than is contained in this niggardly amendment which certainly will prove a disappointment to a great many people.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Martineau in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister whether he has had an opportunity to examine the program that the United States has adopted for its small businesses? When the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was speaking he pointed out the program of assistance under the small business administration in the United States. He said there were 21 different projects which the small business administration of the United States had established to assist small businesses. That is the kind of program, as he pointed out, that the Prime Minister assured the Canadian people he would implement in 1958.
All this is reported in the United States government organization manual for 1960-61. Has the minister had an opportunity to read this report? Can the minister explain to the committee why the government has not accepted this kind of program, particularly in the light of the promise made by the Prime Minister? The minister sits there in solid comfort at the moment and I have a great suspicion-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being five o'clock, the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, notices of motions.

That, in the opinion of this house, immediate steps should be taken by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation either directly or indirectly to provide television to those areas and communities in Canada which are presently denied the enjoyment of such services and facilities.
He said: Mr. Speaker, you have just read the proposed resolution, which I am sure will become a resolution in fact if it is voted upon this afternoon. You will note that it is worded in such a way as to be all-inclusive of areas in Canada which do not now have television facilities and services. Even though the riding of Skeena covers practically one third of the province of British Columbia, the people of that riding have no television whatsoever, and I know there are other regions of British Columbia in the same position. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) told me a moment ago that he too is interested in this matter for the same reason, and the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) also has areas within his constituency that do not enjoy this modern medium of communication.
I raised a similar subject matter in the first session of this parliament immediately after the general election of 1958. In fact it was on June 3, 1958, that I raised the matter by way of grievance following a supply motion. That, of course, did not allow for any vote being taken as to whether or not it was

desirous for the house to give an expression of its opinion. The motion today asks parliament to express an opinion in a formal manner to the effect that steps should be taken to extend television coverage to all areas and communities which are now denied such facilities.
In Skeena we have an estimated population of some 60,000 to 70,000 people and, if allowed, I shall place on the record figures from the 1958 voters lists to indicate the number of registered voters in some of the major communities. Perhaps it would give an indication to the house of what is involved population wise. In my own community of Terrace we had some 2,000 registered voters in 1958; in the Smithers-Telkwa area there were some 1,500 registered voters. In Burns Lake, and in the areas surrounding it, we had another 2,000 voters. The city of Prince Rupert itself, without taking into account the outlying communities, had some 6,000 people on the voters list. In Kitimat there were about 4,300 and in Ocean Falls aproximately 1,400. All these communities have a number of other small communities surrounding them and they are likewise concerned and interested in this particular question. It is almost a perpetual problem and perpetual conflict between those areas which are heavily populated and those which are less heavily populated.
It seems that no matter what type of service is involved, be it highways, daily newspapers, radio or television, the larger populated areas receive them first. For instance, the lower mainland of British Columbia which includes Vancouver, Burnaby and Victoria, is a small area geographically but it contains approximately one half of the population of the entire province, and it is the area which is given prior consideration in any of these matters. In fact this is almost traditional now, and for that reason I believe that a public body such as the C.B.C. should give extra consideration to the outlying areas, the smaller communities and less populated sections of the country. I believe that public agencies such as the C.B.C. should even bend over backwards to ensure that greater consideration is given to providing such services as television in order to balance the scale between the urban and the rural communities.
As a medium of communication television has been in existence for quite a number of years, but as I said earlier we in Skeena do not as yet have the benefit of it. We hope that things will change shortly. As I say, television is considered to be a great means of communication. It has great cultural advantages; and it has great entertainment value. It is true that it also has certain defects and drawbacks, but nothing is either pure black
Request for Extended T.V. Coverage or pure white. Everything that is good contains a little bad, and vice versa.
We do not believe that merely because we do not have a city with a population of 50,000, 75,000 or 100,000 we should be denied services which many people in this nation receive. The needs and the desires of the people in Skeena are just as great as those of the people in Vancouver. I hope the motion before us will be given the due consideration necessary and will receive unanimous passage in the house in order that those who live in the northern parts of the country will understand that parliament itself has concern for our desires and needs.

It is not
very often I agree with the hon. member for Skeena, but on this very point I am in general agreement with the idea he has expressed. My area is very much similar to that which he represents in that it is a big constituency and extends for many miles into the far northern regions.
The idea of a national broadcasting system is one in which the whole nation should participate, but I believe we should realize some of the difficulties in providing television to all areas. Even the royal commission, when it made its study, had this to say:
However much we regret it, there will probably be more than one and a half million Canadians who will have to rely for their broadcasting service on radio and will not in the foreseeable future be brought within reach of Canadian television.
It goes on to say:
We do regret it because the value of television in terms of information, entertainment and identification with the rest of the country is greater for people living in remote areas than it is for Canadians in the settled parts of the country.
I think we can safely say that even today, after having radio service for a good many years, some 2 per cent of the people in Canada do not receive broadcasts from Canadian radio stations. Indeed some of the people who live in the far north will tell you they get Russian broadcasts more easily.
Even though television is a relatively new service in Canada we are rapidly approaching the point when 95 per cent of our people will receive it, but from there on I believe it will be a matter of dollars and cents. In my area during the last few years the government has been trying to work as fast as it possibly can in order to provide that service which the hon. member for Skeena says he needs in his area, and which is needed in many other northern parts of the country.
Only a few years ago there was but a fringe service in the southern portion of my constituency. Considering that my constituency runs about 600 miles north and the

Request for Extended T.V. Coverage fringe reception covers perhaps only 30 miles of the lower portion, one can well understand that it does not serve many people. However, there have been extensions in the last few years. There has been the extension into Baldy Mountain in Manitoba, which has helped many of the people in the southern area and there has also been a steady expansion by the C.B.C. and private stations in the last few years.
Indeed some of the private stations found they could possibly go into the more northern areas of the constituency. As a matter of fact a few years ago the C.B.C. had made application and was prepared to provide service into that area, but because the privately owned stations were willing to do it themselves the C.B.C. withdrew in favour of the privately owned stations, in order that it could conserve funds for areas that privately owned stations could not serve.
I know it is an expensive proposition when one goes into these sparsely populated areas. It is so expensive that for example in the areas around The Pas, which is outside my area, and Flin Flon, which also serves my area, the C.B.C. could not see fit to provide direct transmission because funds were unavailable. In areas such as these you often find that kinerecordings, although perhaps not the best, are accepted.
I can cite examples in my area where within only 20 miles of a signal a community of perhaps 1,000 people will have to go without service until such time as more funds are provided. I think the essence of the whole problem is, where do you gets the funds?
The royal commission reported that in the future there will be demands from areas for two stations. I think this is one factor that should be considered, that before any areas are serviced with two or three stations- many of our residents are serviced to some degree by United States stations, and although this is not the best thing it is not a point of argument-we should service those areas which are without television facilities at the moment. There will be demands in the future from areas which feel that two or three stations can operate quite well and quite profitably, and there will also be demands in the future for an extension of time from those areas which have enjoyed television over the years. This is going to be a factor which will cost money. If there is going to be an extension of time, this will mean that some other areas not now serviced will have to do without television for a longer period. There is also the possibility that the near future will see the advent of colour television.
These are factors at which we must look very carefully, and before we provide these additional services to those areas which are


presently serviced and have been serviced for a good many years we should be very careful about what our policy is going to be and we should be sure that areas that are not serviced do receive some form of television entertainment.
I have taken a few figures from the Fowler commission report and I would just quote three years for which that commission forecast net operating expenditures in this field. They expected that in 1958 the net operating expenditures for radio and television would be approximately $44 million; for 1959, $50 million and for 1960, $55 million. However, the government's estimates for those years were $51 million, $58 million and $62 million. They estimated the capital cost to be $10 million in 1958, $14 million in 1959 and $13 million in 1960. However the government's estimates for those years were $8 million, $9 million and $7 million.
In other words, what I am trying to point out here is that as a result of added operating costs, capital costs have been sacrificed. I think one should look at the operations of the C.B.C. and see that some of the capital expenditures are not sacrificed because of added operating costs. In general I would say that the people of my area want me to support this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I think this resolution will affect a great many people across this country. Because of this I hope that within the short time allotted to its discussion we will be able to come to some decision.
I have before me very detailed information concerning quite a few places in Newfoundland. I am not going to take the time of the house by putting it on the record now, because as I said before I hope that before the hour has expired we will be able to come to some decision. I do feel, however, that since television is in large measure a public service, people living in smaller areas have the same right to expect television service, within reason, as those who live in the more thickly populated areas. I am sure that across this country there are many places that are now not served by television and yet within these areas reside a large percentage of the population of Canada.
I bring to the attention of the house the example of the town of Deer Lake in my own province of Newfoundland. Deer Lake and the surrounding territory has a population of 10,000 people. It is only 30 miles from the larger city of Corner Brook. Corner Brook is a city serviced by television, and yet 30 miles away a town with a population of 10,000 people is not able to receive this public service.

On a number of occasions I have brought to the attention of the house the question of television coverage for Deer Lake. There have been numerous pieces of correspondence on this matter, but so far the service has not been provided for this town. I hope that if this resolution is passed consideration will be given to the justifiable demands which are being made by the people of this important town on the west coast of Newfoundland.
I also bring to the attention of the house a television station which is now being operated at Stephenville, Newfoundland. The station itself and the equipment is owned by the United States forces at Harmon Field, while the station is operated by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Three or four years ago this station was able to serve all the people who were then receiving electric power. Within the last two or three years great strides have been made in this area in extending electric power to many more settlements, and the station at Stephenville is now not able to service all the homes capable of receiving television if such a service were provided. I would hope the time will not be too distant when the station at Stephenville will be either enlarged or relocated so that the service the station provides will have greater coverage than it has today.
In the southern part of what is known in Newfoundland as the Ste Barbe district there is a fairly densely populated area known as Bonne Bay. These people, too, have no television service. I would hope that within a very short time these people will also be able to receive the benefits which come from television broadcasting.
My hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, who is not in the house today because weather conditions have prevented him from returning to Ottawa, has given me a message asking me to state his case for Labrador. In Labrador at the moment there is only one television station, and it is at Goose Bay. Certainly, in this great area other stations are necessary so that service may be provided to all the people concerned.
My hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo, who realizes that in this debate not many people are going to have an opportunity to speak, has asked me to refer to the number of occasions on which he himself has called attention to the need for television coverage of Port aux Basques, Grand Bank and the south coast of Newfoundland. There are in Newfoundland today many places which might well enjoy the advantages which come from television broadcasting and I hope that if this resolution receives the approval of the house these benefits will be brought to the people living in the areas I have mentioned.
Request for Extended T.V. Coverage

First, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the mover of this resolution. I feel it should be allowed to go through. This is something to which a great many people in my own district have looked forward for a number of years.
Before entering upon my talk on this matter I should like to congratulate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation upon the installation of radio stations in the Lake Windermere valley in my area. The residents of this area have been endeavouring over a ten year period to get C.B.C. station programs, programs produced in Canada. Until the installation of the booster last year they were unable to get C.B.C. programs of any kind. This installation was the culmination of many years of effort by boards of trade, chamber of commerce and many other organizations and individuals in the valley. It is fortunate that this government took action at least to provide radio reception, late as it was. It would certainly never have been installed under the previous administration. However, during the period in which the local people in the area were endeavouring to obtain radio reception, television entered the picture. I should also like to mention that at the present time we have a television satellite in the area which will serve a great number of people. We do not know at the present time how many people this will serve, but we feel the coverage will be fairly extensive. However, due to the rocky terrain of the Rocky mountain area in which I live, complete coverage has become impossible with our present facilities.
During the past few months I have been endeavouring to review the work of the C.B.C. and also to study the numerous applications for television services in Canada which have been granted. I find that preference is being given to the larger centres while the rural areas are not getting the consideration that they should be getting. In these days television is not a luxury; it is essential to our way of life, and I suggest that immediate consideration should be given by the minister to the expansion of this television service. A large number of departments and members of parliament have been in receipt of briefs from rural constituencies all over Canada requesting the installation of television satellites to make it possible for people to receive programs without the necessity of installing expensive equipment such as wiring, and having the programs piped in.
I should like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that the installation of television facilities for the larger centres is paid for out of public funds and that the
