Request for Extended T.V. Coverage rural taxpayer contributes heavily to these funds. Therefore, I strongly recommend that before any more applications from the urban centres of Canada are approved, consideration should be given to the installation of television programming for the rural areas. My own area of East Kootenay, as I mentioned, is situated in the heart of the Rocky mountains where television and radio reception is unpredictable. Some of our towns are situated in the valleys and others on the sides of the mountains. A few areas are still without these services. Lake Windermere and the Golden area in the upper end of my constituency have been endeavouring for a number of years to obtain this type of service. In the Fernie area we are fortunate, in one or two cases, to be able to receive programs from the United States, but I think we should develop the distribution of Canadian programs of particular concern and interest to our people. The rural areas are suffering badly from their lack of ability to receive Canadian television.

I am
delighted to rise and support this resolution which has been moved by the handsome, capable and industrious member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). Before proceeding I want to compliment the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. McFarlane) for his completely non-partisan approach to this question and his willingness to support a resolution, moved by a member of this group, which has application all across Canada.
Before going further, I wish to bring to the attention of the house the excellent work that has been done by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) on the radio broadcasting committee with particular reference to this problem and its application across Canada. No one can accuse the hon. member for Port Arthur of being parochial in his approach. I say he has a universal approach to this question and, on occasions, almost a cosmic point of view.
This is a serious problem to numbers of small towns in my constituency. For a number of years I have been urging the government to give effect, through the C.B.C., to what is the spirit and purpose of this motion. Although our larger areas are now served by the C.B.C., including the city of Trail, Rossland and adjacent areas, besides Nelson and the surrounding areas, there are still a number of small communities which are denied the opportunity of receiving C.B.C. programs-the news, music, theatre, ballet and all the other interesting television fare provided by the C.B.C. Because the larger centres now have the opportunity to enjoy


these programs, there is naturally an increasing demand by these other communities for service. We have an area on the west arm of the Kootenay lake which includes Balfour, Procter, Ainsworth, Kaslo and intermediate points which is not served. We have Boswell, Gray Creek, Crawford Bay, Lardeau and Riondel. We have an area around Castiegar, Edgewood, and a considerable area around Slocan city. Residents of these communities and organizations in these centres have written to me consistently in the last two or three years urging consideration of their needs in this respect. To give the house an indication of the type of letters which have come to me, I should like to put on record a letter I have received from Mr. Cyril F. Fitchett who has been very active in travelling around the mountains with officials of the C.B.C., so that when the officials come in to make surveys there need be no unnecessary amount of travelling on their part. I will read what his letter has to say.
Under date of December 22, 1961 he writes as follows:
Dear Sir,
I wish to make a request regarding t.v. reception in this area.
I would appreciate anything you could do to bring C.B.C. television to this district. Unfortunately we are unable to receive any signal from C.B.C. or U.S.A. outlets. I feel we are missing an important part of Canadian life with regard to education, sports, world affairs and drama, in which my wife is particularly interested. She has had, on several occasions, notices mailed to her from C.B.C. t.v. announcing forthcoming drama events and in order to view them we have to drive 20 miles to Nelson, our nearest centre, and impose upon friends. I believe a repeater station is being installed in the Cranbrook area this coming year. Would it be possible to have something similar to serve the people of the Kootenays?
The newly installed radio repeater station at Procter is a great improvement to our reception and I wish to thank you for your help in this regard and for any help you may be able to give us with t.v. service.
Wishing you and your family a happy new year,-
-and so on.
I mention that because it indicates the interest in the C.B.C. and the desire to obtain service. What this gentleman says is repeated in dozens of letters from people who appreciate the low power relay transmitter station for radio which was recently installed and would now like to receive C.B.C. service.
I have taken up this matter with the minister and discussed it with him on a number of occasions. He has been very sympathetic to the problem. We understand from the present debate that it is not a local problem. There are numerous areas in Canada which wish to receive a similar service. I discussed it with the vice president of the C.B.C. and I have written him about it. I have also discussed it with regional officers of the corporation in

Vancouver, with engineers and technicians who have a thorough understanding of the district. All have expressed sympathy with the circumstances that exist and are anxious to do what they can. To that end surveys have been made as to the population, where the repeater stations could be installed, what the approximate cost would be, and so on.
In that connection I wish to quote from a letter I recently received from Captain W. E. S. Briggs dealing with the policy of the corporation which will facilitate the dissemination of the information. Under date of February 13, 1962 he writes:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
This is in reply to your letter of January 30th, 1962, concerning television service for the electoral district of Kootenay West. I believe that a statement of the policies and regulations governing the corporation's program of extending its television coverage would be of assistance to you.
And it has been.
In carrying out its program of extending television coverage, the corporation has made a survey of all unserved areas In Canada. The policy presently in effect dictates that service will be provided on a priority basis to areas where the greatest number of people can be served at the lowest possible cost. The corporation believes that this policy allows the most economical and equitable use of the public funds involved.
A continuing review of all unserved areas is maintained and the priority lists are adjusted from time to time as new information becomes available. As a result of new information provided by the 1961 d.b.s. census figures, a major review is under way of all the unserved areas in Canada.
In regard to the Kootenay West district, you are aware that the corporation presently owns and operates low power radio transmitters at five locations within the district, at Kaslo, Procter, New Denver, Castlegar and Slocan, which provide the C.B.C. national radio network service to these areas. As part of our continuing coverage expansion, an application for another L.P.R.T. in the Kootenay West electoral district, has been filed with the Department of Transport, to provide service for the community of Nakusp.
In case hon. members do not realize it let me say that is my home village. I notice that the Minister of Justice is listening with much interest. I continue:
The C.B.C. national television service is presently being provided for your district by means of C.B.C. owned and operated television stations at Traii and Nelson. Investigations into the possibility of extending this service to other areas in the district, such as Procter and Balfour, have been conducted by our engineers. At the present time, the area of Castlegar is receiving further detailed engineering investigation and preliminary reports appear encouraging for development of a C.B.C. television station for this community.
The corporation has carefully studied the question of monetary participation with private groups in the development of radio and television stations and has concluded that such a policy could not be successfully adopted.
I might say that the community of the Arrow lakes collected money through the
Request for Extended T.V. Coverage community television society, installed equipment on Saddle mountain and is able to receive C.B.C. television service from Kelowna. Several thousand dollars was collected. This was the result of local effort. Other communities cannot do that because the expenditure is larger and the equipment required more intricate and expensive.
As far as regulations are concerned, I am sure you are conversant with the procedure adhered to by the corporation in establishing broadcasting stations. After preliminary investigation of a particular project, the project must receive approval from the C.B.C. board of directors. Following this, detailed engineering studies are conducted and an application submitted to the Department of Transport. The application would then be forwarded to the board of broadcast governors and heard at a public meeting. If recommendation for approval was forthcoming from the B.B.G., it would go forward to the governor in council, who in turn, assuming approval, would issue an order in council to the Minister of Transport for authorization of the station. Only after receiving authority from the minister to establish a station, can the corporation make any commitments for the provision of network service or the purchase of land or equipment. If the equipment to be provided is in excess of $100,000, an additional order in council would be required.
Very frequently, delays of six to 18 months are encountered in the delivery of network service. Because of the corporation's policy to "buy Canadian" whenever possible, and because the specialized equipment required generally has to be especially fabricated, a delivery schedule of nine to 11 months is usually experienced.
In connection with the possibility of providing television service to the Arrow lakes region, the outlook at present does not appear encouraging. Because of the relatively small concentration of population within any one particular service area the very rugged terrain and the estimated high cost of network service, the corporation does not presently have any immediate plans to provide television service to this area.
However, as the national service expands and technical advances are made on equipment particularly suited for small coverage areas, the possibility of bringing service to areas such as the Arrow lakes region offer some promise for the future.
I trust that this somewhat detailed description of the policies and regulations governing the corporation s program of extending television coverage, will be of some assistance to you in clarifying inquiries which may arise.
I quoted that rather lengthy letter because I thought it would be of interest to many people including some hon. members who are taking part in this debate to have an understanding of the procedures of the C.B.C. and the difficulties and regulations with respect to "buy Canadian" and so on.
I am pleased to say that since receiving the letter I have heard that the situation is being reviewed in these areas to determine whether there is some way of providing service at a lower cost than was first estimated. I appreciate the attention of the officials to the problem that confronts the people I represent.

Request for Extended T.V. Coverage
I represent a large productive riding the chief industries of which are mining, lumbering and to a lesser extent agriculture. That means that this government or any government receives considerable revenues in the form of taxation. I believe these people are entitled to receive every consideration particularly since they live in isolated places and are producing the raw materials required to maintain our export markets. All these people are anxious to enjoy Canadian news and Canadian programs in general, including music and drama.
In concluding my brief remarks, therefore, I wish to support all other hon. members who have participated in this interesting debate and urge that every consideration be given by this government to the requirements of the persons who live in the outlying districts and small communities. They should be treated as fairly as those who live in the larger centres.
I know another hon. gentleman behind me is very restless and wishes to participate in the debate, so at this point I will conclude my remarks.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like with the consent of the house, to intervene in the debate for just a few minutes. I do so because several hon. members who have spoken come from the province of British Columbia. I refer to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) who has just taken his seat, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. McFarlane) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I recognize the interest of members from the interior portion of British Columbia especially in a resolution such as this one which urges that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should provide greater television facilities to those areas and communities in Canada which are now denied the enjoyment of such services and facilities.
It was indeed in recognition of the fact that there is a lack of television and radio service in the less heavily settled areas of my province, just as is the case in Canada generally, that it was my pleasure shortly after this government took office and after the Broadcasting Act had been amended, to recommend that there be appointed to the board of directors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a person from the interior area of British Columbia.
I should like to pay tribute to Mrs. R. L. Carter of Salmon Arm for the work she has done as a director of the C.B.C. in successfully urging upon the corporation as a director a considerable number of extensions of services. Indeed, I was discussing with her here in Ottawa recently, on the occasion of the

last meeting of the C.B.C. board of directors, just what was the situation in British Columbia. She gave me some particulars which I regret I have not here with me. She assured me that in the matter of extension of C.B.C. facilities, our province of British Columbia is certainly on an equal footing with if not ahead of any other province in Canada.
I am speaking of the situation over the past four years. I observe my friend the hon. member for Kootenay West nodding agreement.
I know that other members from British Columbia would agree with me that we have been well served in recent years in connection with the extention of facilities. While saying that, however, I recognize the fact that there is still a need to be filled.
I assure my hon. friends and the house that the British Columbia representative on the board of directors of the C.B.C. also recognizes that fact. I can assure at least those members from British Columbia that, in addition to myself, our provincial representative on the board of directors will note with great interest what has been said here as the genuine need for extended services. I shall be glad to make sure that it comes to her attention. I am certain that in it she will find further support for her continuing efforts to persuade her fellow directors of the C.B.C. to meet the very real needs especially of those portions of our province outside of the lower mainland area.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I do not wish to take much time of the house as I hope that a vote can be taken on this motion. Part of the riding which I have the honour to represent in this house is well served by the Timmins station. On the other hand, we have very little French programming. Owing to the fact that the microwave system covers the entire riding from east to west, it is felt-and I think it is only fair to do so- that it should be possible, at rather fair cost, to have installed at two different points satellites which would not only serve the communities along the first trans-Canada highway, namely No. 11-we like to boast about it because it was the first trans-Canada highway ever opened-but also the lumber camps which operate nearly the year around. It would also provide French programming through the C.B.C. French network which, after all, would serve a fairly sizeable part of the population of the riding I represent. I understand that the Ontario Northland Railway have in mind the installation of the microwave system from North Bay to Mooso-nee, or the extension of it right on to Moosonee. There also it would be an improvement for those people in that far distant area to be served by television as well.

I hope that this motion will be considered and voted on before six o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, this debate permits me to raise briefly a problem which has been touched on by other hon. members. It relates to satellite or translator stations in areas which are not properly served by any television station. The problem is pointed up by two areas in my riding, one of which is at Parry Sound town. There the situation was corrected because there was a sufficiently large population to permit a private operator to come in and set up a translator or satellite system economically, to the point where he could justify additional advertising charges by the additional number of homes he could reach. Therefore, in this particular case a private station operator was able to come in and economically instal at his own expense a satellite station for the benefit of the local people.
There is another area which is not quite so fortunate. I refer to Huntsville which is situated on the fringe of at least three stations, none of which gives proper service to a large portion of the area. The problem I wish to mention is this. The private stations can afford to set up a satellite only if they economically can raise their advertising rates to national and international advertisers. If they are trying to give service to a sparsely settled community with perhaps a large area, they hesitate to set up any kind of translator or satellite station because it is not worth their while to do so. If it were a C.B.C. station, the C.B.C. could set up such a satellite, as apparently economic operation is not a primary factor and certainly that is the situation in many locations-but where the primary factor is merely that of providing service to local residents. I believe that some assistance should be given to private television stations in setting up such a satellite. If the private station makes a survey and finds that it cannot do this economically, I think the people who are served by a private station should not suffer because they do not happen to be served by a C.B.C. station. In such a case I think that revenue should not be the prime factor. This is the case in Huntsville where there is no C.B.C. station from which a signal could be received and magnified. The people there have only private stations and none of those at the moment has indicated that it is prepared to go ahead with a satellite.
We are very hopeful that the Barrie station, which is looking into the matter, will eventually do so. However, this did point up one basic difficulty. If a private station has a particular area under its wing it must put in a satellite on an economic basis. On the
Request for Extended T.V. Coverage other hand, if the C.B.C. has an area under its wing it can set up a satellite station at the public expense. Therefore I believe that in such situations some assistance to the private stations should be considered.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) wants to make a few remarks so I will put what I wish to say in brief form. I was very puzzled by the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) in this debate. The gist of them seemed to be that if the lady from Salmon Arm who is on the C.B.C. board of directors is made cognizant of the situation we may get some better development for the future. There is nothing wrong with this, but it would seem to me that it overlooks the part played by a number of members of parliament of all parties, not the least of whom are the hon. member for Churchill and the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Keays), in bringing personally to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its senior executives what the problem is.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, the plain fact of the matter is that we will get an extension of television into the areas about which all of us have been talking when and if funds are earmarked specifically for this purpose and when the whole concept of per capita and per household is put aside for a planned development over five years, let us say, that will attempt to bring television coverage to all those places that are without it. Frankly, the argument of per capita and per household makes very little sense to the people who do not have television. All they know is that they are taxpayers and that extensions are being made in other parts of the country.
This government took the initiative in allowing private television to develop, and in that regard I simply say that we know and recognize that private television will have no part in providing television to those sectors of the country that are asking for it because there is no money in it for them. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has to do the job, in the main, of bringing television to such areas except in the odd, very rare situation where a private station might be closer to an area that is not served. Given this kind of situation, the decision has to be made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as to the amount of money that is going to be spent. Quite obviously the corporation will not extend their budget to the degree that hon. members are talking about and would like because the corporation feels that it is too expensive. I suggest that it is the government's role, and this is not interference for after all the treasury board

Request for Extended T.V. Coverage does go over the C.B.C.'s estimates-earmark specifically an increasing amount of funds to do the job that all of us here recognize needs to be done.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I cannot help saying that I find it regrettable, and I think other members do also who have this problem of communities without television, that in most parts of Canada television is considered to be a much greater need and more desirable than even welfare legislation, government action with regard to unemployment or government action in developing an area in an economic way. It is rather sad that Canadians as a whole give television that high a rating. But these are the facts of the situation and they constitute one of the reasons why I, along with other members who have big hinterland areas to look after with populations scattered in small nodal points, very much wish and hope that the government will support this resolution and do so to the extent of providing more funds to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation specifically earmarked to extend coverage without this formula business that can drag on and on for years, and under which those of us who are outside the corporation have no real understanding and comprehension when our areas are going to get television.

Mr. Speaker, I have a big town in a big district that needs television. There is television all around there but this town does not have it. There is television at the minister's town, Kamloops, and also at Williams Lake, Prince George, Barkerville, which is a suburb, and Wells. I had a letter yesterday from the mayor of Quesnel. These people have been beaten off in their efforts and there has been interference by different parties. The people there want television. They can get it for $12,000 by means of a satellite station but they do not think they should. I have an appointment with Dr. Stewart of the board of broadcast governors to put the claim of these people before him.
Quesnel is one of the oldest towns in British Columbia. It was in existence in the Cariboo in the gold days and it contributed piles of wealth to the government. Therefore I think the people there are entitled to television. There is no reason why they should not have it. They think there is something "screwy" when they cannot get television. This is one of the oldest places in British Columbia. There is no trouble in getting television elsewhere. The people of Kamloops and Prince George have it and I think Quesnel should have it. There is not much more I
can say. I cannot pound it out of the government, but Quesnel is one place that should get television.
I have a long letter here and as I have a couple of minutes left I might read some of it. It reads as follows:
Dear Gus:
You probably will not be surprised to hear from me on the subject of television for Quesnel. You are aware that Williams Lake has "live" television which they obtained by extension from the Kamloops television station. To the north, Prince George has television supplied by CKPG, Prince George, B.C.
About two weeks ago I phoned the manager of the Kamloops television station and asked him if he was interested in bringing television to Quesnel. He replied that he was and that it was entirely feasible from an engineering standpoint. The cost to our town would be approximately $12,000. This expenditure would be necessary because of added antenna, etc. to boost it from Williams Lake to Quesnel. I would like to make it clear at this point that Quesnel wants television quite badly, and "live" television such as Kamloops can supply.
However, since then I had occasion to call Kamloops again and between my phone calls CKPG television, Prince George, has contacted Kamloops and asked them if they were interested in bringing television here. Kamloops replied that they were and CKPG replied they were also interested in bringing television here. Prince George further advised Kamloops that the Department of National Defence or the Department of Transport were putting microwave in immediately between Kamloops and Prince George. Because this was under defence it was supposed to be highly secret. However, Gus, I would like you to find out from from either of these departments if this is correct, that is, are they bringing microwave from Kamloops to Prince George and if so when will it be in operation. Once microwave is in, I am told, C.B.C. can get on it and we can have "live" television without any $12,000 cost.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The house will now revert to the business which was interrupted at five o'clock.

The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. C-49, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act-Mr. Fleming (Eglin-ton)-Mr. Martineau in the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Before the adjournment I had expressed the hope that the

minister was familiar with what they had been doing in the United States in their small business administration. I had suggested it would be worth while noting certain acts which the administration was empowered to do to assist small businesses.
It is empowered to provide financial counselling and to lend to small business concerns to finance plant construction, conversion or expansion, or to finance the acquisition of equipment, facilities, machinery, supplies, or materials, and to supply such concerns with working capital. It is empowered to lend to groups of small business concerns for the purpose of establishing facilities in and through such corporation to produce or secure raw materials or supplies.
It is empowered to make loans to assist small businesses which have sustained substantial economic injury resulting from drought or excessive rainfall. It is empowered to determine what business enterprises shall be designated "small business" concerns with respect to government procurement, lending, disposal of property, and allocation or distribution of materials, or supplies.
The administration is empowered to certify to government procurement officers as to the productive and financial ability of a small business concern to perform a specific government contract. It is empowered to enter into joint determinations with the procuring agencies to set aside for exclusive award to small business concerns the whole or part of government contracts. It is empowered to consult with other government agencies in connection with their issuance of orders or in the formulation of policies affecting small business concerns.
The administration is empowered to approve small business defence production pools to enter into government prime contracts and sublet their performance to small business concerns. They are further empowered to encourage letting of subcontracts by government prime contractors to small business concerns. They are empowered to provide technical and managerial aids to small business concerns, and to inventory productive facilities of small business concerns. They are empowered to consult with government agencies to ensure fair and reasonable treatment for small business concerns.
It is empowered to ascertain and co-ordinate the means whereby the productive capacity of small business concerns can be most effectively utilized.
It is empowered to make grants to state governments, state chartered development credit or finance corporations, colleges, universities, and schools of business, engineering, commerce, or agriculture for studies, research
Small Businesses Loans Act and counselling concerning the managing, financing and operation of small business enterprises.
It is empowered to assist small business concerns to obtain government contracts for research and development. It is empowered to charter and license small business investment companies in order to stimulate and supplement the flow of private equity capital and long term loan funds to small business concerns. It is empowered to make loans to small business investment companies through the purchase of their obligations.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these are some of the things which the small business administration is empowered to do in the United States to assist small businesses. It includes extensions of credit way beyond the terms provided for in this bill and in the act to which this bill is an amendment. It will be seen that what the Prime Minister said in 1957 and 1958 with regard to the plight of small businesses in Canada, and his proposed remedies, as shown in this measure before the house, fall far short of what was promised by the head of the government at that time.
There is no doubt that this is an area in our economy that demands the attention of government. This government has made a start. It has established a small business branch in the Department of Justice-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Justice?
Rather, in the Department of Trade and Commerce.
That shows how much you know about it.

There speaks the Solon from Notre Dame de Grace who wandered into my constituency on Friday last and thereby ensured my re-election, for which I thank him very sincerely.
This small business branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce certainly represents a structure that is far short of what the Prime Minister told us his party would do if it were given an opportunity to form a government. Certainly what the government is doing in this measure falls far short of the requests that were made of the government on September 4, 1958, when a delegation representing the distributive trades advisory committee of Canada, a body which represents the retail, wholesale and manufacturing section of small business, approached the government. It falls far short of what they asked the government to do, and what they asked the government to do is not represented by any substantial means in the amendment that is before the house.
1492	HOUSE OF
Small Businesses Loans Act
This delegation defined a small business as "one with a limited investment that is independently owned and/or employing few people with relatively small sales". The statistics that they produced are relevant to the bill now before us. Unfortunately the minister was not able to give us some of the answers to questions put to him by the hon. member for Peterborough. Those questions are not unrelated to some of the statistics produced in the 1951 census of distribution, which shows the nature of the problem that we face if we really are going to do something to assist small business.
This bill is a misnomer. It suggests that this is not only a measure to provide loans to small business, but by the very use of the phrase "small business" it suggests that the government is embarking upon a wide policy something like that which has been in vogue in the United States now for some time.
But I say the problem in Canada can be ascertained by an examination of the number of retail stores, the number of wholesalers and the number of manufacturers that come within the caption of a small business. We are told that there is one retail store for every 92 inhabitants, one service establishment for every 238 inhabitants, one wholesaler for every 535 inhabitants and one manufacturer for every 378 competitors. We are told that for each wholesaler there are 5.7 retail stores, 2.2 service establishments and 1.4 manufacturers. In all there are some 273,000 business concerns in our country that come under this definition of a small business.
When we recall that this government has provided 3,000 loans totalling some $25 million out of a possible $300 million, we see the inadequacy of the measure now before us. We are told, further, that based on 10 employees or less for retail stores and service establishments, 15 employees or less for wholesalers or manufacturers, 90 per cent in number qualify as small businesses, being approximately 250,000 concerns employing at the peak between 600,000 and 700,000 people, with an aggregate turnover in excess of 30 per cent of all dollar sales; that is $14,404,090,458.
It is partly on these figures that this delegation which called on the government on September 4, 1958 based its claim that small business in Canada was the backbone of our economy. We all recognize that the supermarkets, the discount stores, these corporate enterprises and others provide a challenge and a competition to the small businessman whether he be a wholesaler, a retailer or a manufacturer. If we are going to do something to assist this substantial body of Canadian business people and business institutions,
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1

then certainly we have to do more than this government proposes to do in this amendment or what this government has already done in the main bill of which this measure is an amendment.
I note with some interest that in the representations made by this group, known as the distributive trades advisory committee, they asked not only for credit represented by the maximum of $25,000 provided for under this measure, but they asked for other measures to provide needed guidance on many practical problems such as store arrangement, stock control, accounting, advertising and the like. These measures are certainly not provided by this bill or by this government.

Mr. Chairman, the bill before us has been given second reading and the principle has been approved. It has one clause, and the clause has for its purpose simply the enlargement of a definition in section 2 of the main bill to include within the permissible purposes of loans authorized by the act the relocation of premises.

Mr. Chairman, before you make any ruling, since I believe this is the first time this particular point has arisen since Your Honour became chairman of committees of the whole house, perhaps I should remind Your Honour of what is generally known as the Howard Green principle as applied to the

first clause of a bill, which was insisted upon often and eloquently by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra when he sat on this side of the chamber, when he received very frequently the vocal, and I might even say the noisy and sometimes even the rude support of the hon. member for Eglinton.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only tradition that seems to be involved in the present discussion is the one by which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate seeks to run interference for the hon. member for Essex East and delay the proceedings.
One must protect the weak.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On the point of order, I am sure that none of the hon. members who have spoken on the point would want the debate to be continued in an irrelevant fashion, and I am sure the purpose of all hon. members is to discuss clause 1 in a relevant manner. I was therefore particularly gratified to hear the hon. member for Essex East say he was just reaching the point of relevancy. I hope he has, and that the discussion will continue along that line.
Small Businesses Loans Act

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that you hear well, but I do not think you heard me make the precise point which Your Honour made a moment ago. I have not admitted for a moment that what I have said was irrelevant-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You were out of order.

-but what I sought to imply was that I was now going to deal with something that was more particularly relevant than what I have thus far dealt with. I am sure the Minister of Finance will agree that I have given useful background material to the particular relevancy I am now about to embark on.
The amendment deals, of course, with the conditions under which there will be an extension of further capital made available to small business, and the method of financing small businesses. The brief presented to the government urging the need for a comprehensive small business administration pointed out that an examination of Dun's Review and Modern Industry for October, 1957, showed that in the United States 12.4 per cent of manufacturers, 9 per cent of wholesalers, 9.6 per cent of retailers and 14.1 per cent of service establishments were being held back in their growth by lack of capital and financing. I propose to apply these percentages to Canadian figures, but before doing so I should like to make reference to what the minister said when he introduced this amendment on September 15 of this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have not come to September of this year yet.
Of February, I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

The minister must not think that because I say "September" instead of "February" he has won a point. I expect the Minister of Finance to pay attention to the substance and not to details which are of no consequence.
What substance?

The minister said, if I may refer to his memorable words as recorded on page 915 of Hansard:
From the inception of the act in January 1961 to the end of last December, 2,977 loans amounting to over $25.5 million were made to small business enterprises. Out of total loan disbursements, service businesses accounted for about one half, retail establishments for about one quarter, manufacturers for about one fifth and the remainder of the loans went to wholesalers.
Then he went on to say that the average size of individual loans was $8,000.

We are able to do this from the figures given to the government by the delegation which came to see it in 1958. The delegation points out that in Canada there are 151,626 retailers, and that the number needing capital assistance-

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, your ruling is being cynically defied by the hon. member for Essex East.
I am making my speech. Is the hon. gentleman rising on a point of order?

Mr. Chairman, I think that the question raised by the hon. member for Essex East is particularly relevant because we know that the Prime Minister of this country went across Canada in 1957 and made a great number of promises. I am not going to get into the so-called numbers game with respect to how many have been kept, but certainly one of the promises he made was that he would provide for small businesses laws similar to those that were available to small businesses in the United States. I find that this is a very puny amendment to the act because the Prime Minister said at Camp-bellton, N.B. on May 4, 1957 that he would fashion his small business assistance act upon that of the United States. He said the same thing in Brockville, that action similar to that followed in the United States should be taken in Canada, and so on. I could give many other examples of what he put before the electorate in 1957.
All we got in 1958 was the setting up of the small business branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and it was not until December of 1960 that the Small Businesses Loans Act was introduced. That falls far short of what we know has been available for some years in the United States. In that country even in 1958 they increased the lending authority for a single loan under their small business administration act to $350,000 from $250,000.
There are many other items to which reference could be made. I think particularly of the fact that in the United States legislation there is a maximum rate of interest.

There is no maximum rate of interest in our legislation and it is not provided for in this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GUARANTEE LOANS, ESTABLISH LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the proposed amendments to the Farm Improvement Loans Act will serve to extend the operations under this legislation for a further period of three years. Briefly, it is proposed to provide for a new lending period beginning on July 1, 1962 and ending on June 30, 1965. It is also proposed to establish a limit of $400 million on the aggregate principal amount of guaranteed loans which may be made by the banks during the new lending period.
As hon. members are aware, this legislation is designed to make intermediate term credit more readily available to farmers for the purpose of financing a wide variety of capital improvements. To this end the act authorizes the government to extend a guarantee of 10 per cent of the farm improvement loans made by any one bank in a lending period. To limit the government's over-all contingent liability, the act establishes a maximum on the total amount of guaranteed farm improvement loans which may be made by all banks during the lending period.
The act came into force in 1945 and was given a life of three years. Subsequently it was extended through the addition of new lending periods. The first extension was made in 1948 and further extensions were made in 1951, 1953, 1956 and most recently in 1959. The current lending period, which is the sixth

since the inception of the act, began on April 1, 1959, and runs until June 30, 1962. The maximum on the total principal amount of loans eligible for the 10 per cent guarantee was originally set at $250 million and was increased to $300 million in 1953 and to $400 million in 1961. Originally, the maximum amount which might be borrowed by an individual farmer was set at $3,000; this amount was increased to $4,000 in 1953, to $5,000 in 1956 and to $7,500 in 1959. In reviewing the history of this legislation I might also point out that an amendment was introduced in 1959 to extend the act's coverage to include bee-keepers as eligible borrowers. The two amendments which are now proposed will enable the banks to continue their lending operations under the act for an additional three years.
During the post-war years, technological advance and the mechanization of farms have been dominant features of Canadian agriculture. In this process, farm improvement loans have played a major role by providing the farmer with loan funds, on reasonable terms and conditions, for the purchase of machinery and equipment. For example, in 1960 an amount of $58 million, or considerably more than one half of total farm improvement loans, was used for the acquisition of tractors, combines and hay balers. While the lending facilities under the act have been especially helpful to the farmer for purposes of mechanization, additional borrowing in substantial amounts took place in 1960, as in previous years, and covered a broad range of investment projects including the construction of farm buildings, the purchase of livestock as well as other works for the improvement and development of farms.
The annual report covering the operations under the act for the calendar year 1960 shows that the total amount of loans reached a record level of almost $102 million. There was a further increase in lending during 1961 and for this 12 month period more than 70,000 loans were made amounting to slightly over $108 million. No doubt, if it had not been for the drought in the west, the credit facilities under the Farm Improvement Loans Act would have been used to an even greater extent.
I might add for the purpose of providing a broader perspective on the growth of activities under the act, that during the current lending period from April, 1959 to the end of 1961, over 198,000 loans were made amounting to almost $294 million. This is approximately $55 million, or 23 per cent, higher than the amount borrowed during the whole of the preceding lending period from April, 1956 to March, 1959.

I am sure hon. members will agree that this is a gratifying and enviable record. In this, the co-operation of the banks deserves much credit. Progress under the legislation has, of course, been encouraged by the guarantee on loans as well as the steps taken by the government in recent years to enlarge the scope of the act. I believe the soundness of the operations is attested by the fact that out of total lending of over $1.1 billion since the inception of the act, accumulated losses during this period amounted to roughly $1,356,000 of which some $134,000 has been recovered. Thus, the loss ratio is only slightly in excess of one tenth of one per cent of the total of loans made.
In conclusion, I should like to say that the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act have been of great assistance to Canadian farmers in meeting their credit needs. The government's proposal for extending these operations for a further period of three years will I submit contribute to the wellbeing of our farm population and will help to ensure the development and improvement of Canadian agriculture.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP-SIXTH MEETING- JOINT PRESS STATEMENT

speechtext:
The Canada-United States interparliamentary group concluded two days of discussion in Ottawa today. Twenty three members of the parliament of Canada and 16 members of the congress of the United States, representing all political parties, participated in the discussions. The Canadian delegation was led by the Speakers of the Senate and House of Commons, the Honourable Mark Drouin and the Honourable Roland Michener. The co-chairmen of the United States delegation were the Honourable George Aiken, senator from Vermont and the Honourable Cornelius Gallagher, member of the House of Representatives for New Jersey, assisted by the Honourable Laurence Curtis, member of the house for Massachusetts.
This was the sixth meeting of the group which held its first and organizational meeting in Washington in January 1959. Since that time, meetings have been held alternately in Canada and the United States. The fifth session was held in Washington in June 1961.
The United States delegates were welcomed at the opening plenary session on Thursday, March 1, by the Prime Minister of Canada, Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker.
Committee meetings were held on both days. One committee discussed defence and foreign policy matters of mutual interest and the other discussed economic and boundary matters of concern to both countries. The agreed summary reports of the two committees which were approved at the final plenary session today are attached.
Members of both delegations and their wives were scheduled to leave Ottawa on Saturday morning for Montreal where they will visit the R.C.A.F. air defence command headquarters and attend a reception given in their honour by his Worship the Mayor and Mrs. Drapeau. While in Montreal the cochairmen will visit the city hall to sign the golden book. In the evening the members and their wives will attend a national league hockey game. Both delegations will return to their respective capitals on Sunday.

maintopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON DEFENCE AND FOREIGN POLICY

speechtext:
Berlin and European Security
The committee opened its discussion with a consideration of the status of Berlin and the problem of European security. The discussion reflected no differences of opinion as to the Canadian and the United States approach to the Berlin situation and the basic position
from which any negotiations with the Soviet union should proceed. Major attention, therefore, centred around how the present difficulties arising over Berlin should be approached to reduce tensions with the Soviet union.
The rights accorded the west under the quadripartite arrangements must be maintained. Any search for an accommodation with the Soviet union must take into account three points upon which the west must stand firm-(1) the rights of the people of West Berlin; (2) the rights of the occupying powers to be in the city; and (3) the right of the western powers to have access to the city. Any negotiations with the Soviet union must seek to clarify the latter point so that there will be firm guarantees given the west to have access to the city not only by means of the present four air corridors but also of specific land, rail and water corridors.
The Berlin problem is symptomatic of the many large issues that must be carefully and thoroughly explored, first among the western powers and then with the Soviet union at the diplomatic level before the convocation of a summit conference.
China Policy
The committee noted that since the group's last meeting the question of the admission of a communist Chinese delegation to the United Nations had been considered and had been rejected but that the matter would again confront the next meeting of the general assembly. While neither Canada nor the United States has recognized the Peoples' Republic of China it was reported that there is a body of opinion in Canada which favours Canada granting recognition. There was no disagreement on the need to maintain the integrity of Taiwan but there was some difference of opinion as to the validity of a "two China" policy. The United States members stressed that Taiwan is important to the security of the United States and that the United States administration must always consider the effect of United States recognition on its allies in Southeast Asia, and for these and other reasons the United States opposes such recognition.
There was an extensive discussion of the question of trade with communist China. While there was complete agreement that there should be no trade in strategic goods, the two delegations were not unanimous in

their views as to trade in non-strategic commodities. The Canadian members were generally of the opinion that by such trade it was possible to keep open certain avenues of contact and further questioned the effectiveness of a trade blockade in weakening the position of the Peking regime.
The United States members were of the view that trade with communist China in any form serves to bolster the regime and facilitates its expansionist policies. The United States members, therefore, hope that the free world would be able to co-operate with the United States to the end that nothing be done which would strengthen or hasten the development of communist Chinese military capacities.
Defence Production Sharing
The committee noted the mutual military responsibilities of both countries for the common defence of North America and the endeavours under the Canada-United States defence production sharing program to achieve integration of their defence industries development and production capabilities. The continuing Canadian reliance on United States industry for a substantial part of major items of Canadian defence requirements is economically more acceptable in view of the improving trend of United States defence procurement in Canada.
It was recognized that it would probably never be feasible for the United States to obtain from Canada as large a proportion of United States defence equipment needs as the proportion of Canadian requirements which is purchased from United States industry. The increased participation of Canadian industry in United States defence requirements is achieving an improved pattern of cross-border defence procurement and desirable standardization of equipment. However, this increased activity is revealing difficulties preventing Canadian industry from contributing fully and it was agreed that efforts must continue to ensure that defence industries in both countries have equal opportunity to participate in western defence requirements.
The achievements of the defence production sharing program were commended as an outstanding example of the close cooperation which exists between the two countries and which should continue to receive the active support of both governments. It is important that public opinion in both countries recognize that this program is aimed at more efficient utilization of the industrial capacity in both countries to the benefit of mutual defence and economic interests.
Disarmament
The committee, noting that renewed disarmament negotiations are to begin in Geneva on March 14, expressed the hope that these would result in some progress. It also considered that there were some grounds for restrained optimism in this regard. The committee agreed that initially a good basis for the conference's work exists in the agreed statement of principles and that the participation of foreign ministers would be appropriate to lend additional guidance to the opening phase of the negotiations.
The question of United States resumption of nuclear testing was also discussed. The United States members pointed out any resumption would be undertaken reluctantly and in full awareness of the impact that this would have on public opinion even though devices tested would be held to the minimum in point of number and size. On the other hand the progress which the Soviet union has made in the field of nuclear armaments as evidenced by their series of tests last fall might leave the United States no alternative but to resume testing.
Canada and the OAS
The Canadian delegation expressed its appreciation for President Kennedy's pledge of support to Canada should it desire to become a member of the organization of the American states (OAS). The Canadian members explained the various considerations that have made Canada reluctant to assume the obligations of membership at this time.
It was noted by both the Canadian and United States delegates that Canada has displayed an increased interest in Latin American matters. This has been evidenced by the creation of a Latin American division in the Department of External Affairs, the establishment of diplomatic relations with all the Latin American nations, Canadian membership in the United Nations' economic commission on Latin America, and the assignment of observers at important meetings of the OAS.
There was support for Canadian presence at meetings of the OAS and other interAmerican organizations. It was also suggested that consideration be given to the appointment of a permanent Canadian observer at the OAS.
Cuba
The committee agreed that a communist Cuba is a serious menace in the western hemisphere which requires careful control and counteraction. It was noted that, as a result of recent policy review, the United States had now terminated all imports from

and exports to Cuba with the exception of certain medical supplies. The United States members believed that a similar review and common policy of economic sanctions against Cuba by Canada and all western countries would serve to counter the communist threat. The Canadian delegation recalled that Canada has long since terminated any exports to Cuba of arms, and is rigidly controlling other exports to Cuba and is preventing any re-export of United States goods through Canada. This is a similar policy to that which was recently approved by OAS at Punta del Este.
The committee agreed that the policies of both Canada and the United States must be developed in the light of each country's long-range plans to counter the communist threat.
United Nations Bond Issue.
The committee was unanimous in its support of the United Nations at this difficult juncture in its history. In this connection the committee discussed the method and extent of meeting the United Nations financial obligations arising principally from its efforts to establish peace and security in the Congo. The committee discussed and explored the United Nations proposal to help meet these obligations through the sale of bonds. The failure of many members to meet their assessments has created a financial crisis.
The committee was of the opinion that the United Nations fiscal machinery should be made more efficient and more stringent control should be exercised over financial matters.

Relations with the Common Market
The committee discussed the broad implications and the effects on Canada and the United States of European developments with particular reference to the United Kingdom's application for membership in the common market. The committee recognized that both Canada and the United States face special problems of trade arising from European regional arrangements. At the request of the Canadian delegation the United States delegation outlined the purpose and scope of new trade legislation now before the United States congress. The Canadian delegation expressed support for expansion of multilateral world trade by such measures as may be agreed upon and Canada's willingness to take a constructive part in this expansion.
Both delegations expressed the view that the commercial and agricultural policies of the common market following negotiation for their application to Canada and the United States should result in a fair and adequate access
for the industrial materials, agricultural products and manufactured goods of both countries.
The committee noted the contribution made by the commonwealth and the U.S.A. to world peace and stability.
The Canadian delegation emphasized the significance of traditional commonwealth trade links, including especially free entry into the United Kingdom market and the exchange of preferences. The committee clearly recognized throughout the discussions that it was for the United Kingdom alone to make a decision whether to join the European common market.
It was agreed that Canada and the United States have many common points of view and of interest and that, consequently, in any negotiations and measures undertaken or contemplated by either, this community of interest should be borne in mind.
Columbia River
The Canadian delegation outlined the present situation in Canada with regard to the treaty and1 pointed out that delay of Canadian ratification was related to differences between the federal government and the government of British Columbia. The Canadian delegation noted that it still remains the policy of the Canadian government to ratify the treaty as soon as possible.
The United States delegation observed that the United States had ratified the treaty and expressed the hope for early ratification by Canada. The United States delegation made reference to the urgent needs of the Pacific northwest for power which would require early decisions to be taken on alternative sources of power.
The Richelieu-Champlain Waterway
The committee took up the question of the Richelieu river-lake Champlain waterway. Such a waterway would cover a route of about 400 miles. It would reduce the water distance between Montreal and New York city by 1,200 miles, and between New York city and great lakes ports by a comparable distance.
The United States delegation outlined the history of this proposal, observing that this has been a water route since the earliest days of North America. The United States delegation also noted significant increases in cargo in past years on lake Champlain, and pointed out that development of the waterway would provide considerably greater access to the St. Lawrence seaway.
It was noted that both governments have proposed a joint submission of the question to the international joint commission.
The committee welcomed the report that this matter will be referred to the international joint commission and expressed the

view that the international joint commission should begin a study and submit its recommendations as quickly as possible.
Lumber Trade
The United States delegation noted that recent United States housing legislation has had the effect of increasing the market for lumber in the United States and resulted in the increasing importation of Canadian lumber. As a result the domestic market for United States lumber has been affected. United States shipping legislation (the Jones act) also has had the effect of raising the cost of shipping United States lumber from the Pacific northwest to the eastern seaboard.
There was a frank discussion of the problems outlined by the United States delegation and of the measures which might be taken to alleviate them.
It was apparent that the Canadian lumber industry was not free from problems of competition as well.
Point Roberts
The Canadian delegation outlined the situation that exists at Point Roberts, Whatcom county, Washington, a peninsula crossed by the international boundary (the 49th parallel) isolating the point from the state of Washington. The region is accessible only through Canadian territory or by sea and both countries maintain border crossing points. The area comprises some 5 or 6 square miles
and has a permanent population of some 200 people. Point Roberts is a popular residence for Canadians but difficulties are experienced because of the United States immigration regulations.
United States residents of Whatcom county recently urged the relaxation of United States immigration regulations so as to allow of easier entry by Canadian citizens, particularly those seeking to make the area their permanent residence by obviating the necessity of their becoming United States citizens.
The United States delegation pointed out that the highway between Haines and Whitehorse passes through a section of the Yukon territory making it necessary for people using the road to pass through two separate customs and immigration points.
The committee expressed sympathy for any arrangements which would provide for a satisfactory solution of such problems on the border.
Canada-United States Bilateral Air Agreement
The Canadian delegation drew the committee's attention to delays experienced in continuing discussions with the United States on Canadian-United States air transport relations and pointed out that as a result the Canadian authorities were unable to proceed with current studies of regional air traffic requirements in Canada.
The committee agreed that it would welcome an early resumption of negotiations on the bilateral air agreement.
